stimulus.text:
Senator Henry Cabot Lodge, speech in the Senate on the League of Nations, August 12, 1919 (verbatim excerpts):

"You may call me selfish if you will, conservative or reactionary, or use any other harsh adjective you see fit to apply, but an American I was born and an American I have remained all my life. I can never be anything else but an American, and I must think of the United States first, and when I think of the United States first in an arrangement like this, I am thinking of what is best for the world."

. . .

"I have never had but one allegiance — I cannot divide it now."

The League Covenant's Article X asked member nations to respect and preserve each other's territory against outside attack. Lodge proposed reservations stating that only Congress could commit American forces to such action.

rationales.A: The Senate did vote on the treaty, twice in 1919 and again in 1920. Wilson did not block a vote; he lost the votes that were held.
rationales.B: Wilson did the opposite: he refused the reservations and told loyal Democrats to vote against the treaty with reservations attached.
rationales.C: Background from the books: Lodge's reservations, especially the one protecting Congress's power to declare war, could have won a majority. Wilson refused to compromise and ordered loyal Democrats to vote against the treaty with reservations, so it failed.
rationales.D: Wilson brought the treaty home from Paris and presented it to the Senate. The fight was over the reservations, not over whether the treaty was presented.
rationales.general:
1. Find the middle position. Lodge's reservations could have won a majority in the Senate.
2. Find what Wilson did with it. He refused the reservations and told loyal Democrats to vote against the treaty with them attached.
3. Find the result. With Democrats voting no and the irreconcilables voting no, the treaty fell short of the two-thirds it needed.
Remember: when a measure fails despite a workable middle position, look for the leader who rejected the middle.
